instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data
instruments.status_note: Re-evaluated 21 Oct 2026 (audit item 9): in force with no end of validity and no amending act recorded, per the Publications Office's metadata (Cellar SPARQL, read 21 Oct 2026); general application since 25 May 2018 (Art. 99(2), milestone). Status unchanged. Only the status was re-read that day; the other fields of this record were last re-read on 27 Aug 2026.

dna.objective: Protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data, and free movement of such data within the Union.
dna.risk_logic: Risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: National supervisory authorities with the one-stop-shop for cross-border cases; EDPB consistency and dispute resolution.

sanction_ceiling.note: Two-tier: 2%/EUR 10m for the lower tier, 4%/EUR 20m for the upper tier. The figure recorded is the upper tier.

provisions.heading: Territorial scope
provisions.summary: Applies to processing by a controller or processor established in the Union, and to processing of data subjects in the Union by a controller not established in the Union where it relates to offering goods or services to them or monitoring their behaviour.
provisions.verification_note: Verified 27 Sep 2026 against the Official Journal text (English, retrieved that day from the Publications Office Cellar, CELEX 32016R0679): heading and number match; the summary was checked against paragraphs 1 and 2 (establishment in the Union; offering goods or services to, or monitoring the behaviour of, data subjects in the Union). Paragraph 3 (Member State law applying by virtue of public international law) is not in the summary. The earlier note said the article was recorded from general knowledge.

provisions.heading: Principles relating to processing of personal data
provisions.summary: Six processing principles plus accountability: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality.

provisions.heading: Lawfulness of processing
provisions.summary: Exhaustive list of lawful bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests.

provisions.heading: Processing of special categories of personal data
provisions.summary: Prohibits processing of special categories absent a narrow derogation.

provisions.heading: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
provisions.summary: Protection against decisions based solely on automated processing producing legal or similarly significant effects. In force since 2018, and therefore the pre-existing European law of automated decision-making.

provisions.heading: Data protection by design and by default
Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority
provisions.summary: 72-hour notification decision.

provisions.heading: Data protection impact assessment
provisions.summary: The conceptual ancestor of the DSA's Art. 34 systemic risk assessment and the AI Act's Art. 27 fundamental rights impact assessment.

provisions.heading: Designation of the data protection officer
provisions.summary: Mandatory where processing is carried out by a public authority or body, and in the other cases the Article specifies.
provisions.verification_note: Verified 27 Sep 2026 against the Official Journal text (English, retrieved that day from the Publications Office Cellar, CELEX 32016R0679): heading and number match; the summary was checked against paragraph 1, points (a) to (c): a public authority or body (courts acting in their judicial capacity excepted), regular and systematic monitoring on a large scale, and large-scale processing of special categories. The earlier note said the article was recorded from general knowledge.

provisions.heading: Supervisory authority
provisions.summary: Each Member State provides for one or more independent supervisory authorities.

provisions.heading: Competence of the lead supervisory authority
provisions.summary: The one-stop-shop: the authority of the controller's main establishment leads cross-border cases.

provisions.heading: Cooperation between the lead authority and other concerned authorities
General conditions for imposing administrative fines
provisions.summary: Two-tier penalty ceilings.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on a Single Market For Digital Services
instruments.status_note: Re-evaluated 21 Oct 2026 (audit item 9): in force with no end of validity and no amending act recorded, per the Publications Office's metadata (Cellar SPARQL, read 21 Oct 2026); applicable to all providers since 17 February 2024 (Art. 93(2), milestone). Status unchanged. Only the status was re-read that day; the other fields of this record were last re-read on 27 Aug 2026.

dna.objective: A single market for digital services, replacing the liability core of the 2000 e-Commerce Directive with a graduated due-diligence regime.
dna.risk_logic: Systemic risk (Art. 34), assessed by the provider and mitigated proportionately.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: Commission for VLOPs and VLOSEs; national Digital Services Coordinators for all lower tiers.

provisions.heading: Notice and action mechanisms
provisions.summary: Electronic notice mechanisms for sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated notices. Art. 16(3) provides that a compliant notice gives rise to actual knowledge or awareness for the Art. 6 liability exemption where it allows a diligent provider to identify the illegality without a detailed legal examination.

provisions.heading: Online interface design and organisation
provisions.summary: Ban on dark patterns. Art. 25(2) excludes practices covered by the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive.

provisions.heading: Online protection of minors
provisions.summary: Measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security for minors, including a prohibition on advertising based on profiling where the recipient is known to be a minor.
provisions.verification_note: Verified 27 Sep 2026 against the Official Journal text (English, retrieved that day from the Publications Office Cellar, CELEX 32022R2065): heading and number match; the summary was checked against paragraphs 1 and 2. The Regulation's own threshold for the advertising prohibition is that the provider is "aware with reasonable certainty" that the recipient is a minor, which the summary shortens to "known". The earlier note said the article was recorded from general knowledge.

provisions.heading: Traceability of traders
provisions.summary: Online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders must obtain and check specified trader information before allowing use of the service.
provisions.verification_note: Verified 27 Sep 2026 against the Official Journal text (English, retrieved that day from the Publications Office Cellar, CELEX 32022R2065): heading and number match; the summary was checked against paragraph 1 (information the platform must obtain before a trader may use it to offer products or services to consumers in the Union). The earlier note said the article was recorded from general knowledge.

provisions.heading: Very large online platforms and very large online search engines
provisions.summary: Designation threshold of 45 million average monthly active recipients in the Union.

provisions.heading: Risk assessment
provisions.summary: VLOPs and VLOSEs must diligently identify, analyse and assess systemic risks stemming from the design or functioning of their service, at least annually and before deploying functionalities likely to have a critical impact.

provisions.heading: Mitigation of risks
provisions.summary: Proportionate, effective mitigation, with the choice of measures left to the provider.

provisions.heading: Recommender systems
provisions.summary: At least one recommender option not based on profiling.

provisions.heading: Additional online advertising transparency
provisions.summary: Enhanced advertisement repository.

provisions.heading: Data access and scrutiny
provisions.summary: Art. 40(12) access to publicly available data; Art. 40(4) access to non-public data for vetted researchers, requested through the Digital Services Coordinator of establishment. Both purpose-limited to research on systemic risks.

provisions.heading: Competent authorities and Digital Services Coordinators
Competences
provisions.summary: Allocates supervision between the Commission (VLOPs and VLOSEs) and national Digital Services Coordinators.

provisions.heading: Fines
provisions.summary: Up to 6% of global annual turnover.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector
instruments.status_note: Re-evaluated 21 Oct 2026 (audit item 9): in force with no end of validity and no amending act recorded, per the Publications Office's metadata (Cellar SPARQL, read 21 Oct 2026); applicable since 2 May 2023 (Art. 54, milestone). Status unchanged. Only the status was re-read that day; the other fields of this record were last re-read on 27 Aug 2026.

dna.objective: Contestable and fair markets in the digital sector, through ex ante obligations rather than ex post proof of anticompetitive effect.
dna.risk_logic: Contestability and fairness. Designation is a binary switch, not a graduated tier.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: The Commission is the sole enforcer. National competition authorities may investigate possible non-compliance with Arts. 5-7 on their territory and report to support the Commission (Art. 38(7)); national courts may apply the Regulation in proceedings before them (Art. 39).

provisions.heading: Definitions
provisions.summary: The core platform service categories: intermediation, search, social networking, video sharing, communications, operating systems, browsers, virtual assistants, cloud, advertising.

provisions.heading: Designation of gatekeepers
provisions.summary: Quantitative presumption: substantial EU turnover or market capitalisation, at least 45 million monthly active end users and 10,000 yearly active business users in the Union, sustained over three financial years.

provisions.heading: Obligations for gatekeepers
provisions.summary: Self-executing prohibitions. 5(2) no combining personal data across core platform services without consent, with a genuinely equivalent less-personalised alternative. 5(4) no anti-steering. 5(6) no preventing business users raising non-compliance. 5(7) no requiring use of the gatekeeper's identification, payment or browser engine.

provisions.heading: Obligations susceptible of further specification
provisions.summary: 6(4) third-party app stores and sideloading. 6(5) no self-preferencing in ranking. 6(7) free and effective interoperability. 6(9) data portability. 6(10) business-user access to performance data.

provisions.heading: Obligation for gatekeepers on interoperability of number-independent interpersonal communications services
Fines
provisions.summary: Up to 10% of global annual turnover; 20% on repeated infringement.

provisions.heading: Cooperation and coordination with national competent authorities
provisions.summary: The Commission is the sole enforcer; national authorities support rather than enforce.

provisions.heading: Review
provisions.summary: Required a review by 3 May 2026.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence
instruments.status_note: In force since 2024. Prohibitions, AI-literacy, GPAI duties and governance apply; the high-risk tier does not yet. The scalar alone is insufficient — read the milestones. Re-evaluated 21 Oct 2026 (audit item 9): in force with no end of validity, per the Publications Office's metadata (Cellar SPARQL, read 21 Oct 2026), which records one amending act, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 (the AI Omnibus, amended_by); its application dates are the milestones, re-read against the amended Art. 113 on 14 Oct 2026. Still partly applicable: the high-risk tier applies from 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028. Only the status was re-read on 21 Oct 2026; the other fields were last re-read on 27 Aug 2026.

dna.objective: Harmonised rules on artificial intelligence, structured as product-safety legislation: conformity assessment, technical documentation, notified bodies, CE marking, post-market monitoring.
dna.risk_logic: Four-tier risk pyramid — unacceptable, high, transparency, minimal — with a separate compute-based presumption for general-purpose models.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: AI Office for general-purpose AI models; national competent authorities for AI systems; conformity assessment and market surveillance.

provisions.heading: Scope — exclusion of military, defence and national security
provisions.summary: The Regulation does not apply to AI systems where and in so far as they are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities; nor does it affect Member States' competences concerning national security.

provisions.heading: Definition of a general-purpose AI model
provisions.summary: Displays significant generality, is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks and can be integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications. The Article sets no compute figure: the indicative criterion of more than 10^23 training FLOP comes from the Commission's July 2025 guidelines, not from the Regulation.
provisions.verification_note: Checked 27 Sep 2026 against Article 3, point (63), of the Official Journal text (Cellar, CELEX 32024R1689). The summary used to attach an indicative 10^23 FLOP floor to the Article; the Article contains no compute figure, and that criterion is the Commission's July 2025 guidelines (src-ec-gpai-guidelines-2025). Corrected the same day.

provisions.heading: AI literacy
provisions.summary: Providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and of others operating or using AI systems on their behalf. As replaced by the AI Omnibus, the Article does not require them to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy; the original text required measures to ensure a sufficient level.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal texts read that day from the Publications Office's Cellar: Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (CELEX 32024R1689) as adopted, and Article 1, point (5), of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (CELEX 32026R1744), which replaces it.

provisions.heading: Prohibited AI practices
provisions.summary: Manipulative or deceptive techniques; exploitation of vulnerabilities; social scoring; individual criminal-risk prediction based solely on profiling; untargeted facial-image scraping; emotion inference in workplaces and education; biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes; real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, subject to narrow exceptions. Binds public authorities as well as firms.

provisions.heading: Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
provisions.summary: Two entry routes: 6(1) safety component of a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation; 6(2) falling within Annex III. 6(3) provides a filter where no significant risk of harm is posed, subject to documentation and registration.

provisions.heading: Responsibilities along the AI value chain
provisions.summary: A distributor, importer or deployer becomes a provider — assuming the full obligation set — if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk system, substantially modifies it, or modifies its intended purpose.

provisions.heading: Transparency obligations
provisions.summary: Users must be informed they are interacting with an AI system; synthetic content must be marked in a machine-readable format; deep fakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest must be disclosed.

provisions.heading: Classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
provisions.summary: 51(1)(a) high-impact capabilities or 51(1)(b) Commission decision. 51(2) supplies the operative presumption: cumulative training compute greater than 10^25 FLOP.

provisions.heading: Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models
provisions.summary: Annex XI technical documentation; Annex XII information pack for downstream providers; a copyright compliance policy; a sufficiently detailed public summary of training content. 53(2) partially exempts genuinely free and open-source models, but not systemic-risk models.

provisions.heading: Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
provisions.summary: Model evaluation against standardised protocols including documented adversarial testing; assessment and mitigation of Union-level systemic risks; tracking and prompt reporting of serious incidents; adequate cybersecurity protection.

provisions.heading: Penalties
provisions.summary: Up to 7% of global annual turnover or EUR 35 million.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data
instruments.status_note: General application since 12 September 2025 (Art. 50). The Art. 3(1) design obligation applies to connected products and related services placed on the market after 12 September 2026; the switching-charge ban from 12 January 2027 (Art. 29(1)); Chapter IV's unfair-terms rules to long-running contracts concluded on or before 12 September 2025 from 12 September 2027 (Art. 50). Re-read against the milestones and the Official Journal text (CELEX 32023R2854) on 27 Sep 2026: still partly applicable. last_verified moved from 27 Aug to 27 Sep 2026 on 21 Oct 2026 (audit item 10), the date on which the status above was re-read against Arts 29 and 50 (commit 282a782); the other fields were last re-read on 27 Aug 2026.

dna.objective: Fair access to and use of data — predominantly non-personal, industrial and machine-generated — reallocating control over it by default.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: National competent authorities; penalty levels set by Member States.

sanction_ceiling.note: Set by Member States rather than by the Regulation.

provisions.heading: Obligation to make connected product data accessible to the user
provisions.summary: Connected products must be designed and manufactured so that product and related service data are, by default, easily, securely and directly accessible to the user.

provisions.heading: Contractual terms concerning switching
provisions.summary: Mandatory contractual content for switching: maximum two-month notice period; 30 calendar day transitional period (or a justified alternative not exceeding seven months where technically unfeasible); at least 30 days data retrieval afterwards; full erasure once retrieval ends.

provisions.heading: Conditions under which data holders make data available to data recipients
provisions.summary: Where, in business-to-business relations, a data holder is obliged to make data available to a data recipient, it must agree the arrangements on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms and conditions and in a transparent manner.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32023R2854); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

provisions.heading: Unfair contractual terms related to data access and use between enterprises
provisions.summary: Chapter IV applies to contracts concluded after 12 September 2025, and from 12 September 2027 to contracts concluded on or before that date that are of indefinite duration or due to expire at least ten years from 11 January 2024 (Art. 50).
provisions.verification_note: Added 14 Oct 2026 so that the 12 September 2027 tranche attaches to the chapter it governs. Before this, the 2027 event carried no provision and js/regulatory-model.js read it as the Data Act's GENERAL application date, so Art. 8 (Chapter III) was shown as applying from 12 September 2027 rather than 12 September 2025. Chapter title and Art. 50 read on EUR-Lex (ELI reg/2023/2854/oj) on 14 Oct 2026; Chapter IV consists of Article 13.

instruments.full_name: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union
instruments.status_note: In force since 2023, but a directive: obligations bite at national dates. The transposition deadline of 17 October 2024 has passed and transposition is still materially incomplete: the Commission sent letters of formal notice to 23 Member States in November 2024 and referred Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the Court of Justice in July 2026. Re-evaluated 21 Oct 2026 (audit items 9 and 10): the Commission's July 2026 infringements package (INF/26/1376, 8 Jul 2026) refers Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the Court of Justice for failing to notify complete transposition of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, after letters of formal notice of 28 November 2024 and reasoned opinions of 7 May 2025; the October 2026 package (INF/26/1760) records no closure. Still transposition-overdue. Only the status was re-read that day; the other fields were last re-read on 27 Aug 2026.

transposition.state_note: Only the four Member States referred to the Court of Justice on 8 July 2026 are recorded, because those are the only per-state positions established from a primary source in this build. The remaining 23 Member States are NOT recorded as complete — their status is simply unknown here. A full per-state tracker is required before this field can be presented to users. 27 Sep 2026: the national measures notified to the Commission (Cellar, CELEX 72022L2555*) come from 25 Member States; none from Ireland or Spain, both among those referred. France and the Netherlands, also referred, have notified measures, which shows a notified measure is not complete transposition. The other 23 therefore stay unknown rather than being recorded as complete.

dna.objective: A high common level of cybersecurity across the Union.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: National competent authorities, following national transposition.

sanction_ceiling.note: For essential entities. The provision conferring this ceiling has not been pinned to an article in this build.

provisions.heading: Essential and important entities
provisions.summary: Classifies entities of the types listed in Annexes I and II as essential or important. Annex I entities above the medium-sized-enterprise ceilings, and the special cases the Article lists, are essential; any Annex I or II entity that does not qualify as essential is important. The classification determines the supervisory regime that applies.
provisions.verification_note: Verified 27 Sep 2026 against the Official Journal text (English, retrieved that day from the Publications Office Cellar, CELEX 32022L2555): heading and number match. The previous summary said entities are essential if in Annex I and important if in Annex II; paragraphs 1 and 2 are narrower, and the summary was corrected to them: an Annex I entity is essential only above the medium-sized-enterprise ceilings (or in the listed special cases), and any Annex I or II entity that does not qualify as essential is important. The earlier note said the article was recorded from general knowledge.

provisions.heading: Governance
provisions.summary: Management bodies must approve and oversee the cybersecurity risk-management measures and can be held liable for the entity's infringements (Art. 20(1)); at essential entities, the natural persons responsible can also be held liable (Art. 32(6)). The provision that actually changes boardroom behaviour.

provisions.heading: Cybersecurity risk-management measures
provisions.summary: Ten baseline measures including risk analysis, incident handling, business continuity, supply chain security, cyber hygiene, cryptography policy and multi-factor authentication.

provisions.heading: Reporting obligations
provisions.summary: Early warning within 24 hours, incident notification within 72 hours, final report within one month.

provisions.heading: General aspects concerning supervision and enforcement

instruments.full_name: Directive (EU) 2022/2557 on the resilience of critical entities
instruments.status_note: A directive: obligations bite at national dates. dna.objective: Physical and organisational resilience of critical entities; NIS2's companion on the non-cyber side.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: National competent authorities, following national transposition.

sanction_ceiling.note: unknown — not established in this build.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector
instruments.status_note: Re-evaluated 21 Oct 2026 (audit item 9): in force with no end of validity and no amending act recorded, per the Publications Office's metadata (Cellar SPARQL, read 21 Oct 2026); applicable since 17 January 2025 (Art. 64, milestone). Status unchanged. Only the status was re-read that day; the other fields of this record were last re-read on 27 Aug 2026.

dna.objective: ICT risk management for the financial sector, with no transposition patchwork.
dna.risk_logic: Operational resilience of financial entities and their ICT dependencies.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: Financial supervisors; ESA oversight framework for critical ICT third-party providers.

sanction_ceiling.note: unknown — not established in this build.

provisions.heading: Governance and organisation
provisions.summary: Financial entities must have an internal governance and control framework for the effective and prudent management of ICT risk; the management body defines, approves, oversees and is responsible for the ICT risk management framework.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32022R2554); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

provisions.heading: ICT risk management framework
provisions.summary: Financial entities must have a sound, comprehensive and well-documented ICT risk management framework as part of their overall risk management system.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32022R2554); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

provisions.heading: ICT-related incident management process
provisions.summary: Financial entities must define, establish and implement a process to detect, manage and notify ICT-related incidents.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32022R2554); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

provisions.heading: Reporting of major ICT-related incidents and voluntary notification of significant cyber threats
provisions.summary: Financial entities must report major ICT-related incidents to their competent authority, and may notify significant cyber threats voluntarily.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32022R2554); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

provisions.heading: General requirements for the performance of digital operational resilience testing
provisions.summary: Financial entities other than microenterprises must establish, maintain and review a digital operational resilience testing programme as part of the ICT risk management framework.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32022R2554); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

provisions.heading: General principles (ICT third-party risk)
provisions.summary: Financial entities must manage ICT third-party risk as an integral component of ICT risk within their ICT risk management framework.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32022R2554); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

provisions.heading: Designation of critical ICT third-party service providers
provisions.summary: The ESAs, through the Joint Committee and on the Oversight Forum's recommendation, designate critical ICT third-party service providers and appoint as Lead Overseer for each the ESA responsible for the financial entities holding the largest share of total assets among its users.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32022R2554); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements
instruments.status_note: In force since December 2024. Chapter IV (notification of conformity assessment bodies) has applied since 11 June 2026 and Article 14 — manufacturers' reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents — since 11 September 2026; the Regulation as a whole, including the main obligations on manufacturers, importers and distributors and the reporting obligations of open-source software stewards (Art. 24(3)), applies from 11 December 2027 (Art. 71(2), re-read on EUR-Lex on 14 Oct 2026). The scalar alone is insufficient — read the milestones. last_verified moved from 27 Aug to 14 Oct 2026 on 21 Oct 2026 (audit item 10), the date on which the status above was re-read (docs/AUDIT-2026-10-14.md §1 F), so that it is not earlier than status_as_of; the other fields were last re-read on 27 Aug 2026.

dna.objective: Horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: Market surveillance authorities; coordinated vulnerability reporting.

sanction_ceiling.note: unknown — not established in this build.

provisions.heading: Obligations of manufacturers
provisions.summary: When placing a product with digital elements on the market, manufacturers must ensure it has been designed, developed and produced in accordance with the essential cybersecurity requirements in Part I of Annex I.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32024R2847); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

provisions.heading: Reporting obligations of manufacturers
provisions.summary: Manufacturers must notify any actively exploited vulnerability, and severe incidents, simultaneously to the CSIRT designated as coordinator and to ENISA, via the single reporting platform. Applies from 11 September 2026 (Art. 71(2)).
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32024R2847); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

provisions.heading: Establishment of a single reporting platform
provisions.summary: ENISA establishes the single reporting platform for the notifications under Articles 14 and 15, and manages and maintains its day-to-day operations.
provisions.verification_note: Added 27 Sep 2026 from the Official Journal text retrieved that day from the Publications Office's Cellar (CELEX 32024R2847); heading and summary follow the Article's own paragraphs.

provisions.heading: Obligations of open-source software stewards
provisions.summary: Stewards must have a documented cybersecurity policy and cooperate with market surveillance authorities. Under Art. 24(3) the Art. 14(1) notification obligation applies to them to the extent they are involved in the development of the product, and Art. 14(3) and (8) where severe incidents affect the network and information systems they provide for development. Applies from 11 December 2027, the general date (Art. 71(2)), not from 11 September 2026.
provisions.verification_note: Added 14 Oct 2026 from the Official Journal text read that day on EUR-Lex; the application date is confirmed in the same words on the Commission's CRA reporting page. obligation_on uses actor:pde-manufacturer because the taxonomy has no steward actor; stewards are not manufacturers, and the heading says whose duty this is.

provisions.heading: Notification of conformity assessment bodies
provisions.summary: The rules under which Member States notify the bodies that carry out third-party conformity assessment of products with digital elements. relationships.summary: GDPR Art. 35 DPIAs, DSA Art. 34 systemic risk assessment and AI Act Art. 27 fundamental rights impact assessment are three overlapping assessment duties that regulators themselves acknowledge are duplicated.

Content moderation is processing; ad repositories publish targeting data; Art. 40 access almost always entails personal data. The DSA tells platforms to be transparent while the GDPR tells them to minimise. EDPB guidance mediates the conflict but does not dissolve it.

Both regulate large platforms but on different axes: the DSA on systemic risk and due diligence, the DMA on contestability and fairness. Designation under one does not imply designation under the other.
The DMA operates alongside Articles 101 and 102 TFEU, not instead of them. Google received a separate EUR 2.95 billion Article 102 fine in September 2025.

relationships.summary: The CRA regulates the security of products with digital elements; NIS2 regulates the security of the entities that operate them.

The Data Act mandates open interoperability and the elimination of lock-in; the sovereignty requirements of the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act push toward highly secure, localised environments. The two pull in opposite directions.
The DSA replaced the liability core of the 2000 e-Commerce Directive with a graduated due-diligence regime.

relationships.summary: Almost the entire digital rulebook rests on the internal-market harmonisation competence rather than on a speech, safety or morality competence. That choice shapes each instrument's form.

Article 4(2) TEU reserves national security to the Member States, and the AI Act does not apply to AI systems placed on the market, put into service or used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes (Art. 2(3)). This is the structural source of the asymmetry between constraint on corporate and on state power.
The DSA is without prejudice to the Audiovisual Media Services Directive, which it names first among the acts regulating other aspects of intermediary services.
